primitives.verbatim_quote: ### **<mark>Abstract</mark>** This randomized controlled trial examined whether repeatedsprint training (RST) performed on sand or grass induces different adaptations in collegiate soccer players.
primitives.assumptions: Randomized controlled trial design, matched player populations, equivalent baseline characteristics.

primitives.verbatim_quote: RST within scheduled team sessions improved jump performance, repeated-sprint performance indices, and aerobic fitness in collegiate soccer players, while sand-based training may provide greater benefits for squat jump and selected outcomes related to repeated-sprint fatigue resistance.
primitives.assumptions: Standard RST protocols applied consistently, sufficient recovery between sessions, adequate nutritional intake.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Does not account for overtraining syndrome or detraining effects beyond the study's 6-week window.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core physiological mechanism underlying sand-based RST's superior enhancement in squat jump and repeated-sprint fatigue resistance is the increased mechanical load and reduced ground reaction force absorption on compliant sand surfaces. This leads to greater eccentric muscle damage and subsequent supercompensation in fast-twitch fibers, particularly those contributing to explosive power generation. However, the lack of differential impact on running economy suggests that sand training does not optimize the cost-efficient stride mechanics required for sustained endurance running. Instead, it prioritizes high-force, short-duration outputs. The comparable aerobic adaptations between groups indicate that VO2max and anaerobic threshold are primarily driven by overall training volume and intensity rather than surface-specific perturbations. The statistical significance thresholds employed (p < 0.05) control for Type I error but may underestimate true effect sizes due to modest sample heterogeneity. Future research should incorporate individualized training intensities and longer follow-up periods to assess durability of these effects.
